prompt: Should students be required to learn a second language? Write an essay taking a position.
text:
# Why Students Should Learn a Second Language

Schools should require every student to learn a second language. The requirement costs time and effort, but it gives students skills that few other subjects can match, and it prepares them for a world where crossing cultures is routine.

The strongest argument is cognitive. Learning a language means holding two systems of sound, grammar, and meaning in mind at once. Students must switch between them, notice patterns, and suppress the habits of their first language. Research on bilingual people has linked this practice to stronger attention and better working memory. Some of those findings are still debated, but the broader point holds: few school subjects train the mind in quite this way. Language study also makes students better readers of their own language, because they have to learn what a subject, a tense, or a clause actually does.

A second language also changes how students understand other people. Reading a poem or a news story in its original language shows what translation hides: the jokes, the tone, the words that have no match in English. Students who struggle to say what they mean in a new language learn to be patient with others who face the same struggle. In a country where many neighbors, coworkers, and classmates speak another language at home, that patience has real value.

There is an economic case as well. Employers in health care, law, trade, education, and government often need people who can speak with customers and partners in more than one language. Bilingual workers can stand out in those fields. A graduate who has studied a language for several years starts with a head start, even if fluency still takes more work.

Critics raise fair objections. Many students finish required courses and remember little. Class time is limited, and a language requirement may crowd out art, music, or career training. Some ask why a student who will never leave their hometown should spend years on Spanish or French.

These objections point to problems in how languages are taught, not to a reason to drop the requirement. Students forget their courses when instruction starts late, meets only a few times a week, and focuses on vocabulary lists instead of real conversation. Schools can fix this by starting in elementary grades, when children pick up sounds and grammar most easily, and by teaching through speaking, listening, and use. Schools can also let students choose among several languages, including those spoken in their own communities, so the study feels useful. As for the student who never leaves home, the benefits to attention, reading, and understanding of others apply there too, and no one can know at fourteen where life will lead.

A requirement matters because without one, the students who gain the most are often the ones least likely to choose the subject. Students from families who value languages will study them anyway. Others may never get the chance. Making the subject a standard part of school gives all students the same opening.

Learning a second language is hard, and that is part of its value. It asks students to be patient, to risk sounding foolish, and to keep going until the words come. Schools should require it, teach it well, and start early.
